newsitem.title: USA: Computerized trading the future - Richard Dennis.
newsitem.headline: Computerized trading the future - Richard Dennis.

text.p: Computerized strategies will increasingly dominate trading by commodity and hedge funds, Richard Dennis told the Managed Funds Association conference in New York.
The Managed Funds Association, whose members included Commodity Trading Advisors (CTAs) and hedge funds, was formerly known as the Managed Futures Association until April this year.

"If a computer can now beat the world chess champion, there's no doubt we'll all be computer nerds in ten years time and computerized mechanized trading will be the wave of the future, replacing the discretion of traders," Dennis said.
"Intuitive geniuses are rare and intuition is largely based on experience anyway and intuitive scenarios can be computerized," he said.

Richard Dennis is president of Dennis Trading Group and vice president of C&D Commodities Inc in Chicago, and topped the rankings of commodity funds in 1996 with a 113 percent return, according to fund monitor TASS Management Inc.

Dennis is also well known for a training program for traders, started in conjunction with William Eckhardt, known as the Turtle Trading Program, which advocated a long term volatility break out and trend following system.
"The Turtle Program was a lot less sophisticated than what we are doing now," Dennis said.
"Even if you rely more on fundamental analysis, than technical analysis, that can be quantified and requires systems research, and may be done way better than we're doing it now," he said.
"Fundamental analysis" refers to the economics of supply and demand of a commodity, while "technical analysis" studies price momentum and trends, along with volume and open interest indicators.

"But both fundamental and technical analysts need money management techniques, especially when prices become volatile and price series become discontinuous due to the chaos of wars or catastrophes, and money management principles themselves can be computerized," he said.
"In fact systematic money management techniques are probably more important to trading success than trend definition or trading concepts themselves," Dennis argued.
"It's true though that computerization may already be shortening price trends in financial and commodity markets, as computers help information to get into the markets more quickly."
"But it's unlikely that the optimization of computer programs will ever lead to total randomness in prices, so follow the algorithms," he said.

Dennis argued that the amount of money under management by commodity and hedge funds was being capped by the prolonged boom in equity markets though, as investors felt less need for the diversification provided by commodity markets while the stockmarket uptrend continued.

"So much money is flowing into mutual funds (which invest in stocks and bonds, rather than commodities) that it's the equivalent of a trader showing up every morning at the CME (Chicago Mercantile Exchange) and buying 2,500 S&P500 futures contracts," Dennis said.
"However, I don't believe that recent annual gains in the stockmarket are sustainable forever and valuations look to be way too high," he said.
